title: The whole Gita in one session
word: The whole Gita in one session
hook: eighteen chapters, seven hundred verses, one man in a chariot, in five minutes
tomorrow: Your twelve verses · pick the ones that stayed

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sanjaya's closing. Wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, there is fortune and victory. Your line was victory is there. That was the last verse. This is graduation week. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

Eighteen chapters. About seven hundred verses, as tradition counts them. One conversation in a chariot, parked between two armies. For about seventy days this path has walked through it a few verses at a time, the way a long road trip goes one town at a time: this river, that bridge, the night the car broke down. At the end of a trip like that, it helps to pull over, open the map, and trace the whole route with a finger. That's today. No new verse. The whole route, at once.

One traditional teaching aid divides the Gita into three sets of six chapters. The first six are mostly about action. Chapter one: two armies, and Arjuna sinks down in the chariot. Chapter two: Krishna answers. The self is never born and never dies. You have a right to your action, not to its fruit. Chapters three to five: act, but offer the action. Whenever dharma declines, Krishna says, I come. Chapter six: sit, steady the mind, like a lamp in a windless place. The middle six are mostly about devotion. Chapters seven to nine: Krishna says all this is strung on me like pearls on a thread, and whoever offers a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with love, I accept it. Chapter ten: wherever you see glory, it's a spark of mine. Chapter eleven: Arjuna asks to see, and sees the cosmic form, and is terrified, and asks for the familiar face back. Chapter twelve: devotion, the ladder, and the one dear to me. The last six are mostly about knowledge. Chapter thirteen: the body is the field, and the one light shines in every field. Fourteen: the three threads. Fifteen: the upside-down tree and the highest person. Sixteen: the divine and the demonic, and the three gates. Seventeen: faith follows nature, and om tat sat. And eighteen, the graduation chapter: let go of the fruit, not the act. Reflect fully, then do as you choose. Abandon all dharmas, come to me, do not grieve. And Arjuna stands up. Action, devotion, knowledge. The book weaves them together. That's the word today: the whole Gita in one session.
screen: `ONE TO SIX: ACTION.` · `SEVEN TO TWELVE: DEVOTION.` · `THIRTEEN TO EIGHTEEN: KNOWLEDGE.` · `AND ARJUNA STANDS UP.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE GITA IN ONE SESSION.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture the chariot between the two armies. Arjuna in the back, his head in his hands. Krishna holding the reins. Now let the whole conversation pass through you, without words, just the shape of it. Collapse. Questions. A vision. Love. Understanding. Standing up. Let yourself sit in the chariot for a moment, in the space between the question and the answer. The bell holds the time.
The whole Gita in one session. Eighteen chapters, about seven hundred verses, often read as three sixes: action, devotion and knowledge.

segments.voice: Your line: you read it. Today, tell one person, in one sentence, what the Gita is about. See what you say. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the whole Bhagavad Gita on special days such as Gita Jayanti, sometimes in a single sitting and sometimes over eighteen days, a chapter a day; teachers sometimes divide it into three sets of six chapters.

myth: the Gita has about seven hundred verses in eighteen chapters
one conversation, in a chariot, between two armies.
the three sixes are often labeled action, devotion and knowledge
a traditional way to see the shape of the book, though the themes weave through all of it.
Arjuna asks to see the cosmic form and loves it so much he never wants it to end
chapter 11: he's terrified, and asks for the familiar face back.

fork.setup: in chapter one, Arjuna's bow slips from his hand. by chapter eighteen, what does he say?
options: my confusion is gone; I will do what you say.
fork.reveal: 18.73: my confusion is gone, my memory restored; I stand firm; I will do what you say.

original.note: Sanskrit: bhagavad-gita, the song (gita) of the Blessed One (bhagavan).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gita is a long, complicated philosophy book.
what it means: it's one conversation with a clear shape: collapse, teaching, vision, love, understanding, standing up.
what a scholar hears: the traditional division into three shatkas (1–6 karma, 7–12 bhakti, 13–18 jnana) is a later teaching aid; the Gita sits in the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata.

notes: The three shatkas division (karma, bhakti, jnana): common teaching device; confirm attribution (often associated with Madhusudana Sarasvati) before adding one.
'About seventy days' is approximate (Gita camp began day 157).
Verse count ~700 is standard; some manuscripts differ.
